title: Trump and the Press: A Chronological Ledger, 2015–2026
subtitle: *Working document. Compiled October 26, 2026 from the Trump Tracker corpus, the Deep Dives "Shut Out" data on the 2026 White House press ban, and new research for the periods the tracker covers thinly (the 2016 campaign, the first term, the years between the terms and 2025). Every item carries at least two independent sources or a primary document. Every link comes from the tracker's source lists, the Civics Desk and Deep Dives source files, or a page a researcher loaded and saved, and a script checks each one against that record before the file is accepted. Where the record is an allegation rather than a finding, the entry says so.*

threads.title: Shut Out
threads.dek: Trump banned three news organizations from the White House. Six days later a judge he appointed ordered them back in, and three weeks after that he blocked the ban while the case continues. The claims, the record, and what comes next.
threads.status: The ban is blocked while the case continues; the government has appealed
threads.statusText: On October 13 Judge Timothy J. Kelly granted a preliminary injunction barring enforcement of the hard-pass revocations while the lawsuit proceeds, finding the ban likely unlawful viewpoint discrimination and "practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President's decision." The Justice Department appealed to the D.C. Circuit the next day. The ruling does not address the television pool. On October 26 six readers of White House news filed a second suit, in New York, against the policy as a whole.
threads.question: Trump banned three news organizations from the White House. Six days later a judge he appointed ordered them back in, and three weeks after that he blocked the ban while the case continues. The claims, the record, and what comes next.
threads.answer: On September 18, 2026, the president posted that, "effective immediately," he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The next morning the Secret Service took their reporters' badges at the gate. He named no story. His lawyers later cited national security. A federal judge he appointed found nothing in the record to support that, and ordered the badges returned.

events.title: Trump announces the ban on Truth Social
body: He posted that, "effective immediately," he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" He added: "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow."
He named no story. CNN reported that he did not "identify any specific reporting that prompted his social media declaration."

events.title: In the Oval Office: 'a very simple ban'
body: Asked what the ban would look like, he said, per the Roll Call Factbase transcript: "Oh, the ban on the free press, right? Uh, a very simple ban. I don't want them in my office. I don't want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can."

Asked how it squared with his oath: "Uh, because they're fake news. Uh, you get so tired of reading and seeing fake news." Asked what set it off: "it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it." He said the ban could be lifted if the outlets "could straighten themselves out."

events.title: The correspondents’ association objects, led by a Fox News reporter
body: The White House Correspondents' Association, whose president, Jacqui Heinrich, is Fox News's senior White House correspondent, said: "The WHCA stands in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MSNOW, and POLITICO who are being singled out for doing their jobs."

Ari Fleischer, George W. Bush's press secretary, wrote that he agreed several outlets were biased and unfair, and then rejected the remedy: "Banning them from the WH is not the solution... Don't ban them. Or one day they'll ban us."

events.title: The Secret Service takes the badges at the gate
body: Hard passes were deactivated and physically confiscated at the security kiosk. MS NOW's Akayla Gardner: "officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled. I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

"I asked him if he could provide an explanation as to why it had been deactivated," CNN's Betsy Klein said. "He said he had no further information." Politico's Cheyenne Haslett had her pass taken as well. None of them received written notice or a reason.

events.title: The White House pulls CNN from the television pool
body: The daily guidance removed CNN from the next day's schedule. CNN had been the assigned pool network for Monday and Tuesday, including Trump's address to the U.N. General Assembly. Pool footage goes to the other networks and to "the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN."

events.title: A new reason appears: national security
body: Trump posted: "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS... It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!" CNBC noted that he had not cited national security before.

events.title: The networks refuse to replace CNN
body: Fox News's Washington bureau chief, Bryan Boughton, who chairs the television pool, told subscribers that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President," and that "There will be no replacement pool put in place."

Fox News, ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC said jointly: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting."

events.title: The outlets sue
body: Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump was filed in federal court in Washington, pleading Fifth Amendment due process, First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The complaint opens: "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles."

It was assigned to Judge Timothy J. Kelly, whom Trump appointed in 2017. In 2018 Kelly heard CNN's suit over Jim Acosta's revoked pass and, as ABC reported, "ruled in Acosta's favor after finding that the Trump White House did not afford him proper due process."

events.title: Before any ruling, Trump promises an appeal
body: He posted that the judge "was, sadly, appointed by 'TRUMP.' In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we'll go for appeal."

The White House published a defense titled "White House Access Is a Privilege, Not a Right," which says: "The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool."

body: The Washington Post said it would "not publish any photographs of today's presidential events... until midnight Eastern Time," and Mediaite reported that the New York Times, the Associated Press, Reuters, Getty Images and AFP joined. NPR, a member of the White House radio pool, declined to broadcast audio of Trump.

events.title: The White House launches its own channel
body: It launched "Trump TV," a 24-hour stream of past official clips on the White House's YouTube channel and app. NOTUS reported that its first livestream was a two-month-old clip of the president at Mount Rushmore.

body: Covering him on U.N. credentials, CNN's Kaitlan Collins was told: "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me." Collins said on air that CNN had never said that.
Asked whether he would let the outlets back in if he lost in court, he said the judge would probably rule against him, and: "I think we have a right to clean out fake news."

body: "We're not closing CNN," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on NBC. "There aren't a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it's called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They're just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House."

events.title: The Justice Department asks the court to discard the precedent
body: The government's opposition opens: "After all, access to the White House is a privilege—not a right." On the 1977 case that governs press credentials it does not argue compliance. It argues "that decision is wrong and should be overruled," and says the same of the 2020 appeals-court decision that built on it.
It adds: "At the very least, no injunction may run against the President."

events.title: Four days after the ban, the letters
body: The White House emailed each outlet a letter dated that day, one day after the lawsuit. CNN's arrived at 10:30 p.m. Each says: "This letter is to provide notice that the President has made the determination to revoke hard passes for members of your organization," and sets a deadline: "please submit a written response to us in writing via email by 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, 2026."

No individual signed them. They close "White House Press Office," and they are addressed to the organizations, not to the reporters whose passes were taken. The government's brief calls this "sufficient post-deprivation process."

events.title: Trump calls the judge 'totally disloyal'
body: He posted that the outlets are "sick, treasonous, and demented" and that they have "a great, for them, and totally disloyal Judge." Judge Kelly is a Trump appointee.

events.title: Fifty-one news organizations file against the White House
body: The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents' Association and 49 news organizations asked the court to restore access. Fox News Network is among them. The brief calls the stated reasons "transparently viewpoint discriminatory" and says "unassailable First Amendment law makes any viewpoint-based decision to bar reporters from a nonpublic forum constitutionally repugnant."

events.title: The hearing: 'I have to apply them'
body: Judge Kelly told the government he is bound by the cases it wanted discarded: "Maybe they were, maybe they weren't, but currently as a district judge I have to apply them." On the record before him, due process "wasn't followed here." On the letters: "I don't know [that] a letter they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of standards that they'd have to conform their conduct to."
He did not rule from the bench, and said he would decide "as soon as I can."

events.title: Two of the accusations come apart
body: The Associated Press reported that an anonymous-source story cited against Politico "appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House itself." The Washington Post, which reviewed a recording of the call, reported: "The Associated Press, Bloomberg and CNBC were among several outlets who reported on the call, citing a senior administration official, but were not banned from the White House."

MS NOW's Washington bureau chief swore that of the three MS NOW articles the letter cites, only one was written by a journalist who held a White House hard pass, and that pass was renewed a week after the story now cited against the network.

events.title: The order: 'full stop'
body: Judge Kelly granted the temporary restraining order and directed that the passes be restored immediately. To the argument that Sherrill and Karem were wrongly decided, the order answers: "Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop."

He found the government's only standard "is so vague it hardly does the trick," and that "[N]othing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns." The order runs fourteen days, binds the defendants "except for President Trump," and was not stayed.

events.title: Turned away at the gate anyway
body: Journalists from all three outlets were refused entry. Betsy Klein was denied at 9 a.m., and her request to have her pass back was refused. The outlets filed an emergency notice: "Defendants have already repeatedly violated the Court's Order," adding that the government's lawyers had not responded to a request to call the judge together.

events.title: The passes come back
body: Kelly ordered the government to answer by 12:30 p.m. The White House's press operations director, Micah Stopperich, filed a sworn timeline: her team was told shortly after 7 a.m. to turn the badges back on, and the Secret Service indicated shortly after 9 a.m. that the passes were "back on." CNN and MS NOW journalists were admitted at noon. Politico said its access came that afternoon.

The judge accepted the explanation and declined to hold an emergency hearing. He set the next stage, with a motion for a preliminary injunction due September 28, and said the court "intends to rule expeditiously."

events.title: In the Oval Office with Xi, photographers only
body: The meeting with Xi Jinping had been scheduled as closed press. At the last minute the White House admitted still photographers only and "denied requests from the rest of the pool, including reporters who would be asking questions, to join." In front of the photographers, Trump remarked that Xi has the friendliest press corps in the world. The Associated Press added: "China is one of the most oppressive environments for journalists in the world."

events.title: 'They refused to be there'
body: Trump posted that CNN and "MSDNC" "refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years," Xi's morning arrival. CNN called the claim false. Xi arrived at about 10 a.m.; CNN's Betsy Klein was not let back onto the grounds until around noon, and both networks covered the arrival on their digital platforms. The television pool, CNN included, did not film it because the networks were still waiting for the White House to confirm that CNN could take its turn.

events.title: Kept out of the state dinner arrival
body: Xi's evening arrival was open to pre-credentialed media, a wider group than the pool. About an hour before he was due, CNN reported, the White House said it could cover the arrival with a photojournalist and an audio technician only, while other networks were permitted reporters and producers. MS NOW's Laura Barrón-López said she was told she could not be let in.

The White House's rapid-response account wrote, "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call." The restraining order restored the hard passes; whether it reaches event credentials is unsettled, and Deadline noted that the evening exclusion "does not appear to be addressed in Kelly's order."

events.title: The pool comes back
body: The network television pool, paused since September 21, resumed. CBS had the White House duty and CNN the in-town pool at the National Archives, where the networks carried its feed of Trump and Xi. CNN anchor Pamela Brown: "CNN's access to the White House has been restored, and the TV pool appears to be functioning as normal." The outlets' lawyer, Ted Boutrous, said they believe pool access "is covered by the temporary restraining order."

events.title: 'It's been very fair'
body: At a tea meeting with Xi and the two first ladies, Trump said, "And we appreciate the fair coverage. It's been very fair."

events.title: CNN is left off Air Force One
body: Guidance issued the night before left CNN, the scheduled television pool network, off the plane for Trump's trip to a college football game in Knoxville. The seat "has long been saved for a member of the U.S. network video pool," the Associated Press reported, and the guidance "included Real America's Voice," which is not part of that group. CNN reported that "No outlet was listed as replacing CNN." Aboard, Real America's Voice's correspondent said, "CNN is not here; we have taken over that responsibility." The restraining order "said nothing directly about Air Force One," the AP noted.

events.title: "FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE!!!"
body: Trump posted: "Why should perpetrators of FAKE NEWS, like CNN and MSDNC, be allowed access to a very sacred place, the White House?" An hour and a half later: "FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE!!! IT HAS GONE ON FAR TOO LONG, AT A TREMENDOUS COST TO OUR COUNTRY." A third post, about coverage of his endorsement of Byron Donalds, named eight news organizations and said they "should not be allowed to enter the White House premises, or Press Room, because they are CORRUPT and DISHONEST!"

Leaving for Knoxville, he was asked by MS NOW's Akayla Gardner, "Do you only want outlets that support you to be a part of the press pool?" He answered, "No, no, no. I want real news, not fake news — like you." When she asked whether he did not want tough questions, he cut her off. In the transcript Gardner published: "Wait, wait. Quiet."

events.title: The networks go back to work, around CNN
body: The New York Times, citing four people briefed on the decision, reported that the networks were "set to resume their collective television coverage" even though the White House blocked CNN: "Each time that CNN came up in the pool rotation, the group of networks would decide whether to provide a substitute crew. Otherwise, CNN's slot would be left unfilled."

events.title: The attorney general: "a privilege and not a right"
body: On ABC's "This Week," Attorney General Todd Blanche said, "Well, the president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it," and, "It is a privilege and not a right to be there." Asked by Martha Raddatz for an example of CNN reporting inaccurately: "You cannot be asking me that." Raddatz: "The president said nothing about national security when he announced this ban."

events.title: The outlets ask for an order that lasts until the case is decided
body: Late on September 28, CNN, MS NOW and Politico asked Judge Kelly for a preliminary injunction to replace the restraining order, which expires October 8. "The White House's words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity," the filing says. It adds that after the order the administration kept confiscating passes on September 24 "before finally coming into compliance roughly 11 hours after this Court's order," and it puts the Air Force One exclusion before the court. The ACLU of D.C. filed in support the next day: "The White House is the people's house, not the president's private golf club."

events.title: The judge blocks the ban while the case continues
body: Judge Kelly, a Trump appointee, granted a preliminary injunction, an order that holds until the case is decided. "The record is clear that President Trump made the decision at issue," he wrote, and, "Freed from such a naiveté, it is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him." His conclusion: "Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination." On the government's security rationale he found "practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President's decision."

He added a caution in the other direction: "no one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded."

body: "The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office," a White House spokesperson said. The Justice Department filed a notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit.

events.title: CNN tells the Justice Department it will go back to court
body: The White House kept CNN off Air Force One for a weekend trip to Georgia and Florida. CNN's lawyer, Ted Boutrous, wrote to the Justice Department: "These efforts to retaliate and discriminate against CNN based on the content of its news coverage are mistaken, counterproductive, and unlawful." take: The government’s case came down to one request: that a trial judge treat two appeals-court decisions as wrongly decided. A district judge cannot do that, as this one said at the hearing and again in his order, so the argument was addressed to a higher court from its first page.

What the six days exposed matters more than the ruling. The stated reason moved from fake news, to national security, to decorum, each arriving after the one before it had been tried. When the cited stories were checked, the list included the government’s own preliminary finding, the words of its own official at a public meeting, and a background call the White House set up itself.

A press office that cannot name the rule a reporter broke has not enforced a rule. It has chosen who is allowed in the room, which is the thing the First Amendment exists to prevent. It is worth noticing who signed the brief saying so: Fox News.

corrections.text: The tracker entry this page draws on originally said the phrase "ban on the free press" appeared in no transcript of Trump's remarks. chapters.title: The 2016 campaign, June 2015 to January 2017
prose: As a candidate, Trump made the press a target of the campaign itself: his campaign barred outlets by name, a Spanish-language anchor was removed from a press conference, and Trump promised to change the libel laws so he could sue. These are a campaign's acts, not a government's; the government's begin with the inauguration.

chapters.title: First term, January 2017 to January 2021
prose: In office, the attacks continued in words, from "the enemy of the American People" to calls to challenge network licenses, and moved into the machinery of government. The Justice Department seized reporters' records in leak cases; the White House revoked or suspended press passes until courts ordered them restored and ended the daily briefing; agencies took down data, and NOAA disavowed its own forecasters; and the head of the government's international broadcasters fired the networks' leaders and investigated Voice of America journalists for bias. Courts ruled against the administration in the press-pass cases, in Portland and at the Agency for Global Media.

chapters.title: Between the terms, January 2021 to January 2025
prose: Out of office, Trump took the press to court. He sued the New York Times, CNN, Bob Woodward, ABC, CBS and the Des Moines Register. The Times and CNN suits were dismissed in 2023 and ABC settled in December 2024; the CBS suit was settled, and the Woodward and Register suits dismissed, after he returned to office. As a candidate he said reporters who would not name their sources should go to jail and that networks covering him critically should lose their licenses, and his campaign barred reporters whose coverage it disliked. As president-elect, in December 2024, he said the suits should have been brought by the Justice Department.

chapters.title: Second term: 2025
prose: The second term opened with the FCC reviving complaints against three networks and investigating NPR, PBS and a radio station over its reporting, the AP barred over "Gulf of America," the White House taking control of the press pool, and Voice of America's staff sent home. The attorney general rescinded protections against subpoenaing reporters, Congress at Trump's request rescinded the Corporation for Public Broadcasting's funding for 2026 and 2027, and federal officers used force against journalists covering immigration protests in Los Angeles and Chicago; judges issued orders restraining them. In the fall the FCC chairman's warning to ABC's affiliates preceded Jimmy Kimmel's suspension, and nearly every outlet in the Pentagon press corps turned in its badges rather than accept its credential rules.

chapters.title: Second term: 2026
prose: In 2026 the leak investigations reached reporters directly: the FBI searched a Washington Post reporter's home, and prosecutors subpoenaed reporters at the Times, the Journal and the Post. Federal agents arrested journalists covering immigration protests, the Pentagon barred reporters from its press office and kept them under escort, and the FCC chairman warned broadcasters over their war coverage and their polls. In September Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House; a judge he had appointed, in a preliminary ruling the government has appealed, found the ban likely to be unlawful viewpoint discrimination.

intro: **What counts here.** An act is included when Trump, his White House, his campaign acting for him, or an appointee acting in office took it against the press or against the public's access to government information. Each entry carries the one label that fits it best:

**Who counts as the actor.** Trump himself, including as a candidate in 2015–16 and 2022–24 and as a private litigant between the terms; his White House and campaign; and his appointees acting in office (the FCC chairman, the attorney general, the FBI director, the secretaries of defense and homeland security, the head of the Agency for Global Media). Republicans in Congress, state and local officials, and the outlets' own decisions are left out unless a government act drove them and a source says so. Appendix A lists what was weighed and left out, with the reason.

**Status language.** "Ruled" names the court and the ground. "Dismissed" says on what ground; a dismissal on standing or for failure to state a claim is not a finding that the reporting was false or true. "Alleged" means the claim rests on reporting that has not been confirmed by a finding, and the entry names the outlets and whether the sourcing is anonymous.

**Ratings.** Items drawn from the Trump Tracker carry its severity rating (catastrophic, severe, serious, moderate, concerning) and a link to the tracker entry, which has the full account and the complete source list; the date shown is the tracker entry's date. Items added by new research, or drawn from the Deep Dives data, carry no rating.

**Overlap with the corruption ledger.** The settlements that media companies paid Trump also appear in `trump-corruption-chronology.md`, as pay-to-play. Here they are counted as acts against the press.

**Years.** Dates are the date of the act where known, otherwise the date it was first reported. A matter that ran on (a suit, a ban and the rulings on it) appears at the date of the act, with the outcome in the same entry.

labelDefs.label: Access and the pool
labelDefs.meaning: Rules for who covers the president that apply to everyone: pool selection, seating, ended or cut briefings, removing the press from workspaces.

labelDefs.label: Bans and credentials
labelDefs.meaning: A named outlet or reporter shut out, or a credential rule whose effect is exclusion: revoked passes, barred outlets, the Pentagon pledge.

labelDefs.label: Lawsuits and settlements
labelDefs.meaning: Suits by Trump, his campaign or his company against outlets, pollsters, authors and publishers; his government's suits to stop books; legal threats in writing; and what was paid to settle.

labelDefs.label: The FCC and licenses
labelDefs.meaning: Acts of the FCC and its chairman: license threats and early reviews, investigations of newsrooms, merger reviews and conditions that reach coverage, and pressure on the commission's own members.

labelDefs.label: Public media and Voice of America
labelDefs.meaning: The Corporation for Public Broadcasting, NPR and PBS; the U.S. Agency for Global Media, Voice of America, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Radio Free Asia and the Open Technology Fund: defunding, firings, shutdowns, and the rulings on them.

labelDefs.label: Threats and rhetoric
labelDefs.meaning: Statements that threaten a consequence (jail, prosecution, a lost license, a lawsuit, a firing) or single out a named reporter or outlet. Generic "fake news" posts are not itemized; published tallies of them are in Appendix B.

labelDefs.label: Leak investigations and subpoenas
labelDefs.meaning: Seizures of reporters' records, subpoenas and gag orders, changes to the Justice Department's rules on subpoenaing the press, and leak hunts aimed at the press.

labelDefs.label: Action against named journalists
labelDefs.meaning: Official action rather than words: investigations, arrests, detention, deportation, visa actions, border screening, firings at a government-funded outlet, and force used by federal agents on reporters.

labelDefs.label: Information withheld
labelDefs.meaning: Public data, records, reports and briefings removed or stopped: website and dataset purges, firing or overruling statistics and science officials over published findings, records rules weakened, reports withheld.

The White House's January 6 website, its 24-hour "Trump TV" stream and the crowd-size claims of January 2017 are government messaging, not withholding ([tracker](https://thetrumptracker.com/controversy?id=jan6-website-historical-revisionism), [tracker](https://thetrumptracker.com/controversy?id=white-house-launches-trump-tv-24-7-stream-after-press-ban), [tracker](https://thetrumptracker.com/controversy?id=inauguration-crowd-size-lies)). setAside.head: The Epstein files.
setAside.text: The tracker holds more than twenty entries on the Justice Department's handling of the Epstein files. They concern a criminal case's records and a transparency law Congress wrote for them, and they are tracked as their own story. One is kept in the body because it is a court finding about public access: Judge Sullivan's ruling that the department had conceded it was violating the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

setAside.head: Researched leads set aside.
setAside.text: The research agents' reports list every lead they could not bring to the standard (two independent sources or a primary document) or that fell outside the scope test; the main ones are these.

setAside.head: The campaign and the first term.
setAside.text: The Justice Department's 2017 demand that AT&T sell CNN as a condition of the Time Warner merger was reported by NPR, but the court found AT&T had "fallen far short" of showing selective enforcement and the company dropped that defense, so the record does not establish an act against CNN. The May 2020 executive order on "online censorship" and the withdrawal of FCC Commissioner Michael O'Rielly's renomination concern social-media platforms, and sources disagree on why the renomination was withdrawn. The campaign's June 2020 demand that CNN retract a poll rests on USA Today alone, and Michael Pack's withholding of visa extensions for foreign journalists at the government networks on NPR alone. Trump's praise in 2018 of Rep. Greg Gianforte for assaulting a reporter is in the tracker entry on the CNN wrestling video. The prosecutions of sources such as Reality Winner and Terry Albury, and the 2019 Espionage Act indictment of Julian Assange, were not researched for this ledger; they are candidates for a later pass.

setAside.head: Between the terms.
setAside.text: Trump's July 2021 suits against Twitter, Facebook and YouTube over his removal are against platforms, not the press; their 2025 settlements are counted in the settlements entry. Vanity Fair's accounts of Trump throwing NBC reporter Vaughn Hillyard's phones aboard his plane (March 2023) and of the campaign cutting off credentials for Washington Post, Axios and other reporters (April 2024) rest on that one outlet. The campaign's January 2024 denial of credentials to two Globe Gazette journalists was reversed the next day. The ten-page letter from Trump's lawyer demanding $10 billion from the New York Times and Penguin Random House in late October 2024 rests on the Columbia Journalism Review's review of it. Kash Patel's December 2023 vow that a second Trump administration would "come after the people in the media" was made when he held no office, and the campaign distanced itself from it. Trump's designations of Brendan Carr to chair the FCC (November 2024) and Kari Lake to lead Voice of America (December 2024) are appointments; what each did in office is in the body.

The disappearance of the EPA's EJScreen tool is documented by an advocacy group and one outlet, with no record of the decision. The Pentagon's March leak investigation with polygraphs, and the attempt to keep CNN's Haley Britzky off a Hegseth trip (one underlying report), were aimed at staff or rest on a single source. The State Department's trimmed human rights reports concern the content of a report, not its release. Carr's refusal of a bipartisan petition to repeal the FCC's news-distortion policy changed nothing. The Justice Department's partial release of the Epstein files on the statutory deadline belongs with the Epstein files (see above). Single-sourced: the acting U.S. attorney in Albany removing the Times Union from his press list (the paper's own report; reversed overnight), the closure of Voice of America bureaus in December (one secondary source), the State Department's day-pass rule for reporters (RSF only), the Wall Street Journal kept off Air Force One for the Asia trip (RSF only), and Trump's July 2 suggestion that reporters be made to reveal sources (Washington Post only). The pardons of people who attacked journalists on January 6 have no label here and the count was not verified.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's April 7 statement that the department would subpoena reporters rests on the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker's account alone. The Pentagon's polygraphing of about 50 Joint Staff members in a leak inquiry rests on anonymous sourcing and was aimed at officials, not reporters. The detentions of Luis Galeano and Wilmer Solano Davila in immigration actions are not tied by any source to their journalism; the New Jersey State Police's arrest of Trisha Brownlee is a state act; the actor in a stun-grenade injury in Minneapolis on January 11 is disputed; and FBI agents' questioning of an Oregon photographer about protesters' identities was described by the Tracker as "not threatening or coercive." Court rulings in 2026 on acts of 2025 (the Voice of America and NPR-PBS cases, the Pentagon credential rules, the New York Times and CNN suits) appear in the entries for those acts. The AP's appeal over its exclusion from the Oval Office was argued in November 2025 and is undecided.

method:
**What was read.** The ledger was built on October 26, 2026 from three bodies of material. First, the Trump Tracker corpus: every entry was searched by id, title, `specialTags` and summary for press, media, FCC, public-media, leak, credential and public-information terms, each candidate was read, and an entry was kept only when Trump, his White House or an appointee acting in office was the actor. Sixty-eight entries were kept; those weighed and dropped are in Appendix A. Second, the Deep Dives "Shut Out" data on the September 2026 White House press ban, which supplied two items and the outcome of the ban. Third, new research for the years the tracker covers thinly.

**Tracker items.** Each keeps the entry's date, its severity rating and a link to the entry, which carries the full source list. The one or two sentences after the title were written from the entry's own text, and its three best sources were chosen for document type (court records and government documents first), relevance to the act, and a spread of outlets. Two entries were checked against primary records and corrected here (see below).

**Research.** Five research agents, each assigned a period (2015 to 2020; 2021 to 2024; January to June 2025; July to December 2025; and a narrow 2026 pass for acts the tracker lacked), worked from a written set of rules: two independent sources or a primary document for every item, the outcome of every matter where there was one, verbatim quotations only, and the exact headline of every page cited. Each agent loaded every page it cited, saved its text under `press-chronology/research/<period>/`, and listed it in that folder's `map.tsv`. Every quotation in the researched items was then checked by script against those saved texts. The first-term president's tweets are cited to the American Presidency Project's daily compilations; his Truth Social posts are quoted from outlets that reproduced them, because trumpstruth.org refuses automated access. Paywalled pages were cited only where the headline and opening loaded.

**Merging.** Each act appears once, at the date of the act, with its outcome in the same entry: rulings, settlements and later developments are folded into the entry for the act they concern. Repeated statements of the same threat within days are given as one entry. Where the tracker holds a later development as an entry of its own (the dismissal of a suit, a later ruling), both are kept and cross-referenced. Researched items that duplicated a tracker entry were dropped. Two items carry month-only dates because the record gives no day.

**The rhetoric rule.** Statements are included when they threaten a consequence or single out a named reporter or outlet. The label as first proposed covered named reporters; named outlets were added during the merge so that statements such as "the enemy of the American People," which named five networks, could be included.

**The URL gate.** `press-chronology/gate.py` checks every link in this file against the union of the Trump Tracker's sources, the Civics Desk and Deep Dives source lists, and the agents' `map.tsv` files; it also checks that every tracker link names an entry that exists and that no item title contains an em dash. It exits non-zero on any miss. On the final run it checked 716 links, 586 of them distinct source URLs, and found no misses.

**Tracker discrepancies found.** `bls-commissioner-fired` dated the firing of Erika McEntarfer August 15, 2025; the Bureau of Labor Statistics release and same-day reporting put it on August 1, and this ledger uses that date. `trump-epstein-wsj-defamation-lawsuit-dismissed` presented the defendants' arguments (falsity, malice and damages) as the judge's findings; the order rests on actual malice and special damages and "declines to address" truth and defamatory meaning. `ej-antoni-bls-nomination` was dated August 1, 2025; the nomination was announced August 11 and withdrawn September 30. All three entries were corrected on October 27, 2026, each with a dated correction note. In `media-tech-settlements-86-million-trump-library-ballroom`, one CNN citation carries a headline that differs from the page it links to.

**Limits.** The tracker is dense only from 2026, so the earlier years rest on research that is necessarily selective; the agents' search budgets were capped, and some leads could not be sourced to the standard (Appendix A). Counts of attacks and incidents published by press-freedom groups (Appendix B) include acts by local police and are not added together. Sources documenting single-outlet or anonymous-source claims are named in the entry. The researched URLs were loaded by the agents that cited them, and the tracker URLs come from the tracker's own source lists; the gate proves where each link came from, not that every page will stay up.
